bull_thesis: The bull case is that this is a great operator being punished for a commodity price it does not control, and that the commodity will mean-revert. Xiaomi's problem is precise and external: artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory chips, pushing DRAM and NAND contract prices to roughly four to five times year-ago levels. Memory is about 60% of the bill of materials on a budget phone, so the pass-through was brutal — first-quarter 2026 revenue fell 10.9% to RMB 99.1 billion and net income fell 57% to RMB 4.72 billion (reported 26 May 2026). Nothing in that sentence is about customers wanting less Xiaomi. Memory is the most reliably cyclical input in electronics; every supplier now has maximum incentive to add capacity, and when the cycle turns, the earnings that vanished come back roughly as fast as they left. Underneath the squeeze the franchise is intact and, in places, still compounding. Full-year 2025 revenue reached RMB 457.3 billion, up 25%, with adjusted net profit of RMB 39.2 billion, up 44%. The car business went from nothing to 410,000 deliveries in 2025 against a 300,000 target — a 37% over-delivery — and 185,055 more in the first half of 2026. Premium phones reached 27.1% of China sales, and the company shipped its own 3-nanometer processor, putting it in a club with Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and MediaTek. Management has committed RMB 200 billion of research spending for 2026-2030 and RMB 60 billion to artificial intelligence over three years, funded from a genuine net cash position of RMB 66.8 billion (RMB 102.05 billion of cash against RMB 35.25 billion of debt at 31 March 2026). This is a balance sheet that can wait out a cost cycle, and management is using it: about 399.6 million Class B shares were repurchased for roughly HKD 14.6 billion under the prior programme, a fresh HKD 20 billion authorisation took effect on 2 June 2026, and an automatic HKD 4 billion tranche began on 19 June 2026 — the company is buying its own stock into the drawdown. The valuation is not demanding on any normalised measure: at RMB 23.72 the shares trade at about 18 times trailing earnings of RMB 1.32 per share, or roughly 16 times after stripping the RMB 2.57 per share of net cash. If memory normalises by mid-2027 and earnings return to the RMB 1.50-1.70 range, a 16-18 times multiple puts the shares meaningfully higher, with the car business and any eventual artificial-intelligence monetisation as unpaid options on top. The conditions this case requires: memory supply must actually loosen on roughly the expected schedule; Xiaomi must hold its share position through the squeeze rather than buy it back with permanent margin concessions; and the car business must return to the profitability it briefly demonstrated in the third and fourth quarters of 2025.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that the memory squeeze is not the problem but the diagnostic — it revealed that Xiaomi has no pricing power, and the market has not finished repricing that discovery. A company with a real moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it, and lost the volume anyway: first-quarter 2026 shipments fell 19.2% to 33.8 million units, the steepest decline among the top five global brands, while Samsung and Apple — who face the identical input inflation with deeper balance sheets and real pricing power — took share. Operating profit fell about 70%. The connected-devices segment fell 24% to RMB 24.7 billion as Chinese trade-in subsidies faded, removing a prop that had flattered 2025. The car business, the entire growth story, returned to a RMB 3.1 billion operating loss on 20.1% gross margin (down from 23.2%) — about USD 5,600 lost per vehicle versus roughly USD 900 a year earlier — after only two profitable quarters. The returns evidence says this was always the case: return on invested capital is 8.0% and return on equity 10.9% after five years of 20%-plus growth. Xiaomi has never earned an excess return on capital; it buys share and volume. That reframes the 22.3% gross margin of 2025 as a cyclical peak rather than a base — consistent with margins sitting 1.16 standard deviations above their own historical peak — and it means normalised earnings may be materially below what the bull case extrapolates. Management's credibility on this specific variable is spent. On the first-quarter 2025 call, handed the question directly by Citi's analyst, Lu Weibing said the memory cost increase would be 'a rather slow increase', that 'I do not think the increase will be very drastic', and that smartphone gross margin was 'controllable and stable'. He repeated the reassurance in August 2025: 'on the cost end, we have not seen big changes or big change variables.' By the March 2026 call the same team conceded 'it is very difficult to foretell early on, like what we had been able to do before.' A live commitment now rests on that broken forecasting: management said in March 2026 it was 'fully committed to delivering 550,000' cars in 2026, but 185,055 units in the first half means the second half must nearly double — the first unreachable target in the company's public record, from a team that had trained the market to expect over-delivery. Strategically, the squeeze is already destroying franchise value, not just earnings: the flagship Xiaomi 18 Ultra was cancelled outright over memory costs, decapitating the premiumisation thesis at its apex, and analysts expect the constraint to persist through mid-2027. Meanwhile the cost base is committed and rising — RMB 40 billion of research spending guided for 2026 into collapsing profits, with Caixin reporting staff cuts across divisions since March toward a preliminary ~30% target that the company calls routine. Free cash flow had already fallen 33% before the shock. What confirms the bear: the second-quarter results due in late August 2026 showing continued margin compression, and the 550,000 car target being walked back. The deepest problem is that none of this resolves on anything Xiaomi does — it resolves when memory loosens, a date owned by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, already pushed out once.
consensus_delta: For a name tagged deep value, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. Here the answer is the opposite of the one the tag implies, and that is the whole finding: the market has not capitulated at all. The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high above HKD 61, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy, against an average twelve-month target of HKD 39.52 — roughly 44% above the HKD 27.50 at which the Hong Kong dollar counter trades. Only three say sell. A 54% drawdown with an intact buy consensus is a falling knife, not a fear-print. So where we disagree with the market is not the direction the street is looking — it is that the street has not yet marked its own model. Three specific consensus assumptions are factually strained. First, that average target embeds a 550,000-car year, because that is the number management committed to on 24 March 2026 and no one has been told otherwise. First-half deliveries of 185,055 require the second half to deliver about 365,000 — nearly double the run rate — and Jefferies' Edison Lee (Underperform, HKD 25.49, cut from Hold) and a 14 July sell-side downgrade citing exactly this are so far the only voices marking it. The target is anchored to a number that will be revised. Second, consensus treats the memory squeeze as a one-to-two-quarter dent. The dated evidence says otherwise: DRAM and NAND at four to five times year-ago levels, contract prices up roughly fivefold for phones and tenfold for televisions, memory at ~60% of budget-device bill of materials, and analysts now placing normalisation at mid-2027 — a date already pushed out once. That is three to four more quarters of compression, not one. Third, and most subtly, the street models this as a margin dent while treating market share as stable. It is not: shipments fell 19.2% in the first quarter, the worst of the top five, and reporting on 15 July confirms share slipping to Samsung and Apple. Xiaomi is paying the cost shock and losing the volume — the worst of both. Our honest counter-position: we are not more bearish than the price. We are more bearish than the consensus that sits behind the price, and the gap between HKD 39.52 and reality has to close before this becomes interesting.
forcing_function: There is no hard date, and that is the disqualifying feature. The re-rating driver is memory normalisation, and it has all four marks of a soft, non-binding catalyst: it is owned by third parties (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron), it is undated, it is a commodity cycle rather than a contractual event, and it has already been pushed out once — from an implied second-half-2026 recovery to analyst expectations now clustered at mid-2027. There is no contract, no deal term and no scheduled decision that pays anybody anything. What the calendar actually offers, in order: the interim results in late August 2026, which are a dated event but a negatively-skewed one — the most likely content is another compressed quarter plus the walk-back of the 550,000-car target, which forces a re-rating downward, not up. Beyond that, the electric-vehicle business is scheduled to enter Europe in 2027, and management has said artificial-intelligence commercialisation is 'too early to talk about' — an explicit statement that the option has no exercise date. The HKD 20 billion buyback is the closest thing to a company-controlled catalyst, and it has already fired: it was authorised on 2 June 2026, the automatic tranche began 19 June, and the stock made new lows anyway. A catalyst that has run without effect is spent. The honest forcing function for this name is a memory spot-price roll-over confirmed by supplier capacity guidance, plus a reset car target that consensus has actually marked to — and the right posture is to watch for both rather than to pay for them in advance.
valley_of_death: For a deep-value name the question is whether an event kills the thesis before the discount converges. There is no solvency question here — RMB 66.8 billion of net cash and no maturity wall mean Xiaomi cannot be forced into anything. The risk is entirely that the next three to nine months keep resetting earnings downward while the memory clock runs. Four dated things sit in that window. First and largest, the second-quarter and interim results due in late August 2026 (our data shows the next report about 41 days out): the memory squeeze was in full effect for the whole quarter, the connected-devices business laps the expiry of Chinese trade-in subsidies that flattered 2025, and the car division enters with unit economics of about USD 5,600 lost per vehicle. There is no mechanism by which that print is good. Second, the 550,000-car target has to be walked back, most likely at those same interim results or at the third quarter — the first guidance cut in this management's public record, from a team that had trained the market on over-delivery. That is a credibility event, not just a numbers event. Third, the premium mix deteriorates on a cancelled product: the Xiaomi 18 Ultra was scrapped over memory costs, so the second half loses its halo flagship while the Redmi Note 17 (launched 14 July) and the SkyNomad SUV (unveiled 14 July) ship into an inflated bill of materials. Fourth, the cost base is committed and moving the wrong way — RMB 40 billion of research spending guided for 2026 and RMB 60 billion of artificial-intelligence investment over three years, sized in a fatter-margin world, against free cash flow that had already fallen 33% before the shock. The Caixin report of staff cuts since March toward a preliminary ~30% target, which the company calls routine, suggests the internal view of the squeeze is more severe than the external guidance. And the macro overlay cuts against the entry: our regime read places a hawkish Fed under Warsh with roughly 77% odds of a hike by December, which is a headwind for a long-duration Chinese growth multiple. The thesis does not die in this window. It just gets cheaper, and the cheapness that matters arrives after the guidance cut, not before it.
positioning_washout: The candid answer is that there is no washout here, and its absence is a large part of the case for waiting. The mechanics that normally force selling are all missing. There is no dividend to cut, so there is no yield-focused holder base to be mechanically ejected. There is no covenant, no maturity and no rating trigger, because the company sits on RMB 66.8 billion of net cash. Xiaomi is a major constituent of the Hang Seng, Hang Seng China Enterprises and Hang Seng Tech indices, so a large slice of the register is passive and will not sell on fundamentals — it will only sell if index weights fall, which is a lagging consequence of a lower price rather than a cause of one. And the single largest identifiable flow is pointing the other way: the company itself is a price-insensitive buyer, with roughly HKD 14.6 billion of Class B shares already repurchased under the prior programme, a HKD 20 billion authorisation live from 2 June 2026 and an automatic HKD 4 billion tranche running since 19 June 2026. That is support, not pressure — though at roughly 3% of market value it is a cushion, not a floor, and it has manifestly not stopped the stock from making new lows. What has not happened yet is the real washout: the holder base is still substantially made of growth and momentum money that owns this as a Chinese artificial-intelligence and electric-vehicle winner. The label is in the process of inverting to artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure victim, and that re-labelling — not a margin call — is what would force the rotation. It typically completes on a guidance cut, which is exactly what the 550,000-car target sets up for late August. One execution note specific to this listing: the renminbi counter (81810.HK) traded about 310,000 shares against 319 million on the Hong Kong dollar counter (1810.HK) in the same session. This counter is thin to the point that position size is constrained regardless of the view, and it prices at roughly a 5% discount to the Hong Kong dollar counter's currency-adjusted level — a real consideration for entry and, more importantly, for exit.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now — a good company, a real drawdown, and the wrong trade at this price. Xiaomi is not broken. The 2021-2025 record is genuine (revenue compounding to RMB 457.3 billion in 2025, up 25%; a car business from zero to 410,000 deliveries against a 300,000 target; a shipping in-house 3-nanometer processor; RMB 66.8 billion of net cash), and the thing hurting it is external and cyclical: artificial-intelligence data centres outbidding phone makers for memory, with DRAM and NAND at four to five times year-ago levels. That is a cost shock, not the death of demand, which is why we call the structural threat manageable rather than terminal and refuse to file this under artificial-intelligence displacement. Nobody buys fewer phones because of a chatbot. But three things stop this from being a buy, and they compound. First, the arithmetic. Our parts-based fair value is about RMB 26.00 against a live RMB 23.72 — roughly 10% of upside — while the adverse case sits at RMB 15.50, about 35% below. Risking three to make one is not value investing, it is hope with a spreadsheet. The shares fell 54% and are still only fair. Second, the market has not capitulated. Twenty-three of thirty analysts still say buy, with an average target of HKD 39.52 against HKD 27.50 — a target that embeds a 550,000-car year that first-half deliveries of 185,055 have already made unreachable. Deep value requires the street to have surrendered; here the street has not yet marked its own model, so the next revisions are still downward. Third, and decisive under the current regime: this thesis resolves on one shared macro factor that Xiaomi does not control. Owning it is a short position on the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure cycle in consumer-electronics clothing — the same factor our regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, and the identified driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23-25 June. The regime rewards hard-dated catalysts and structural special situations in thinly-covered lanes, and penalises theses that hinge on a single shared driver arriving on schedule. This name is the mirror image of what the regime wants: thirty analysts, no hard date, and a recovery clock owned by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron that has already slipped once, to mid-2027. The moat read confirms the discipline. The memory shock ran the experiment for us: a wide-moat company passes a cost shock to customers, and Xiaomi ate it and lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple. Eight percent return on invested capital after five years of superb growth says this was always a narrow moat with an eroding trend, and that the record 22.3% gross margin of 2025 was a cyclical peak, not a base. On valuation alone, ignoring every catalyst and the regime entirely, the value case rates a 2 — about 10% below our own fair value, on collapsing earnings and a return on capital that has never exceeded its cost, is roughly fair, not cheap. What would change this: a memory spot-price roll-over confirmed by supplier capacity guidance, a reset car target that consensus has actually marked to, and a price closer to RMB 18-19 where the adverse case is covered and the recovery is free. The late-August interim results are the event to watch — most likely another compressed quarter plus the first guidance cut in this management's record. That is the flush worth waiting for. Buy the wash-out, not the fall.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Xiaomi Corporation (81810.HK / 1810.HK)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-16 · **Transcripts reviewed:** 2024-11-18 (Q3 2024), 2025-03-18 (FY2024), 2025-05-27 (Q1 2025), 2025-08-19 (H1 2025), 2026-03-24 (FY2025) · **Price used:** RMB 23.72 on the renminbi-traded counter (81810.HK); the Hong Kong dollar counter (1810.HK) trades at HKD 27.50.

**Bottom line up front:** Xiaomi's management delivered spectacularly on everything they controlled — smartphone share, premium mix, and a car business built from nothing to 410,000 deliveries in under two years. They were then wrong, repeatedly and with unusual confidence, about the one variable that has since destroyed half the share price: the cost of memory chips. The execution record is genuine. The forecasting record on inputs is broken, and management has now said so themselves.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not so much shift as **compound, then crack**.

**Late 2024 — the three-curve story.** Lu Weibing closes the Q3 2024 call by naming "three growth curves that have already been completed": phones/tablets/wearables, then large home appliances, then vehicles. Revenue was RMB 92.5 billion, up 31%, and the car business had just crossed 100,000 units in 230 days. The tone is a company that has found its formula and is repeating it.

**Early-to-mid 2025 — the hard-tech escalation.** The story widens from "we make good products" to "we are a foundational technology company." The Q1 2025 call is where the ambition peaks: the XRING O1 3-nanometer in-house phone processor, an open-source large language model, and a five-year research budget stepping from RMB 102 billion (2021–2025) to **RMB 200 billion (2026–2030)**. Lu is explicit that financial discipline is subordinate: "today, we are investing without much consideration about cost."

**Late 2025 — the ecosystem/AI layer.** By the FY2025 call (2026-03-24), the emphasis has moved again, to artificial intelligence and robotics: a trillion-parameter model, RMB 60 billion of AI investment over three years, and factory robots. Revenue crossed RMB 400 billion for the first time (RMB 457.3 billion, up 25%), adjusted net profit RMB 39.2 billion, up 44%.

**The quiet crack.** The growth drivers were never dropped — they were overtaken. What changes tone in the FY2025 call is not the strategy but the **admission of forecasting failure on memory**, and one telling aside from Alain Lam: "The second half of 2025 was more challenging [than] the first." The smartphone-and-connected-devices segment grew only 5.4% for the year — the engine that funds everything had already stalled while the AI narrative was being scaled up.

**What is missing from every transcript.** These calls end in March 2026. The Q1 2026 collapse (reported 2026-05-26) is **not in this transcript set** — the story management tells here is one whose central assumption had already failed by the time the market heard about it.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (quarter) | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Gross margin… controllable and stable" for smartphones; memory cost increase "will be a rather slow increase… I don't think the increase will be very drastic" (Q1 2025, 2025-05-27) | Memory contract prices rose **roughly 4–5x year-on-year** for phones and ~10x for TVs; memory is ~60% of the bill of materials on budget devices. Q1 2026 operating profit fell ~70% | **Refuted, decisively.** The single most consequential forecast on the tape, and it was wrong by an order of magnitude |
| "On the cost end, we haven't seen big changes or big change variables" (H1 2025, 2025-08-19) | Two quarters later: revenue −10.9%, net income −57% | **Refuted.** Not a one-off slip — the same reassurance was repeated across quarters |
| "We are fully committed to delivering 550,000 units" of cars in 2026 (FY2025, 2026-03-24) | H1 2026 deliveries **185,055** (+17.2%). Reaching 550,000 needs ~365,000 in H2 — roughly double the first-half rate | **On track to miss**, and the market has not yet been told |
| Revenue and profit at record highs; "high-quality growth" (FY2025) | FY2025 revenue RMB 457.3 billion (+25%), net income RMB 41.6 billion; 5-year EPS CAGR +19.7%, book-value CAGR +16.8% | **Corroborated.** The 2021–2025 record is real and strong |
| Cars: 2024 target 130,000 → 2025 target 300,000 | Delivered ~136,000 then **410,000** — a 37% over-delivery | **Over-delivered.** Elite execution on the thing they controlled |
| Premiumization is working; share of RMB 4,000–6,000 phones tripled in five years (FY2024) | FY2025 premium models 27.1% of China sales, up 3.8 points; global ASP at records | **Corroborated** — but the memory crunch has since forced cancellation of the **Xiaomi 18 Ultra flagship**, which attacks this thesis at its apex |
| "Our strategy… 20% GP margin" and it will hold (Q1 2025) | FY2025 gross margin 22.3% — a record. Then Q1 2026 crushed it | **Held until the input shock, then broke** |
| Cars have reached "economies of scale… quite satisfactory gross margin" (H1 2025) | EV segment made its first profits in Q3/Q4 2025 — then **returned to a RMB 3.1 billion operating loss in Q1 2026**, about **USD 5,600 lost per car** versus ~USD 900 a year earlier | **Corroborated, then reversed** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** Two places. First, returns: for all the record revenue, **return on invested capital is 8.0% and return on equity 10.9%** — this is a company that has never converted its scale into high returns, and the narrative's confidence is not matched by the returns evidence. Second, cash generation: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of RMB 20.8 billion against RMB 41.6 billion of accounting profit, and free cash flow **fell 33% year-on-year** while the story got louder. The car and chip ambitions consume the cash the phone business earns.

**A correction to our own inputs.** The screener's headline numbers on this name are unreliable and should not be used. The scan's "Fair Value 5.79 / Margin of Safety −96%" and "P/FCF 199.1x" cannot be reconciled with the scan's own trailing data: at RMB 23.72, the RMB 613 billion market value against RMB 20.79 billion of trailing free cash flow is about **30x free cash flow**, and trailing earnings of RMB 1.32 per share put the stock at **about 18x**, or ~16x after stripping the net cash. A discounted-cash-flow model that returns a −100% margin of safety on all five methods is registering the car-and-chip capital spending as permanent value destruction, not reading a real signal. The honest bear case here is **not** that the stock is at 199x cash flow — it is that trailing multiples flatter a company whose earnings are actively collapsing.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining** — and the decline is concentrated almost entirely in the last call.

- **Q3 2024 — offensive, expansive.** "We have unlimited potential." "Shopping malls love us." Lu answers a store-count question by raising the target mid-answer.
- **FY2024 — peak conviction.** "The future of Xiaomi is full of infinite possibilities and imagination." Specific, numeric, forward-leaning.
- **Q1 2025 — peak confidence, and the fatal call.** "The key word for results was record high." This is also the call where Lu waves away memory costs and says of the chip programme, "we do not pay much attention to financial targets."
- **H1 2025 — still offensive, with one honest retreat.** Unprompted, Lu corrects his own prior claim on air conditioners: "Let me first correct myself. We are not really #1… There is still a big gap from #1." That is a real green flag; executives protecting a narrative do not volunteer this.
- **FY2025 — the tone breaks.** The language turns defensive and, for the first time, uncertain: "it's very hard for us to quantify that… it is very difficult to foretell early on, **like what we had been able to do before**." And: "In the short term, there may be some pressure on our business." On pricing, the framing shifts from confidence to triage — "we want to maintain our market position," which is the language of defending share, not harvesting it.

The specificity of guidance also inverts. Through 2024–2025 management gave hard numbers freely (store counts, delivery targets, research budgets, share-point goals). On the FY2025 call, asked directly about gross margin and pricing, the answer is qualitative and hedged. When a management team that has been unusually numeric goes vague on the one number that matters, that is information.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** The record splits cleanly in two, and the split is the whole story.

**On outputs — things Xiaomi controls — reliability is High.**

| Guided | Given | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 car deliveries 130,000 | Q3 2024 | ~136,000 ✅ |
| 2025 car deliveries 300,000 | FY2024 | **410,000** ✅ (+37%) |
| 15,000 stores by end-2024, 20,000 by end-2025 | Q3 2024 / FY2024 | ~15,000 confirmed FY2024 ✅ |
| 2025 research spend RMB 30 billion | FY2024 | RMB 33 billion ✅ |
| China share +1 point per year | Repeatedly | Returned to **#1 in China** in Q1 2025, +4.7 points ✅ |

**On inputs and margins — things Xiaomi does not control — reliability is Low.** The memory call was not a near-miss; it was confidently wrong, restated across at least two calls, and it is the direct cause of a 54% drawdown.

**On the reported beat rate.** Our data shows beats in only **1 of the last 3 quarters (33%)**. This does not sit comfortably beside the over-delivery record above, and the reconciliation is instructive: Xiaomi beats on **volume** and misses on **profit**. That is precisely the signature of a company whose costs, not its demand, are out of its control.

**Sandbagging pattern: yes, on volumes, and it has now inverted into its opposite.** Management habitually set delivery targets it could beat (300,000 → 410,000). The 2026 target of 550,000 breaks that habit — with 185,055 delivered in H1, this is the first time in the record that Xiaomi has publicly committed to a number it looks unable to reach. A management team that has trained the market to expect over-delivery is now set up to under-deliver. That reversal is worth more than the target itself.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question they got right and management got wrong.** Citi's Kyna Wong, on the Q1 2025 call, asked directly: "there are other memory vendors who are adjusting their capacity and that will impact the overall supply situation. So, in this regard, will you change your previous view?" Lu declined: "our judgment is that we are quite accurate in our judgment… the impact on Xiaomi will be controllable." **The analyst saw it a full year early. Management dismissed it.** This is the single most important exchange in the transcript set.

**Deflections that recur:**
- **Gross-margin mechanics on cars.** Asked repeatedly (Xu Yingbo, H1 2025) for the cost bridge, the answer is "we do not have much incremental information. Our gross margin is quite good." The EV segment then posted a RMB 3.1 billion loss.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrates with the funding need.** Track the load-bearing noun by call: *stores and share* (2024) → *chips* (Q1 2025) → *AI and robots* (FY2025). Each new frontier arrives with a bigger number attached (RMB 50 billion for chips → RMB 60 billion for AI → RMB 200 billion for research). The pattern is a company that answers a maturing core business by opening a new frontier. Sometimes that is visionary. It is also, mechanically, how returns on capital stay at 8%.

**"Scale and profit" quietly became "maintain our market position."** In FY2024 Lu described a philosophy shift from "scale first" to "long-term sustainable high-quality growth." By FY2025, under cost pressure, the revealed priority is share: "we want to maintain our market position. That is very important to us." The 2022-era philosophy did not survive its first real test.

**A new voice, less certainty.** The FY2025 call is partly answered by an "Unknown Executive" rather than the usual Lu/Lam pairing, and it is that voice which delivers the memory-cost capitulation. Note also the interpreter's currency errors throughout the earlier calls ("JPY365.9 billion" for RMB) — a transcription artifact, not a signal, but a reason to trust the reported financials over the transcript text.

**The tell they did not intend.** Lu's own cost taxonomy on the FY2025 call — memory hurts "smartphone, notebook and also tablets" most, "less so for smart cars… and even less so for IoT" — is management ranking its own segments by vulnerability. It confirms that the profit engine (phones) is the most exposed part, and that the car business, the growth story, is the *shelter*. That is the opposite of how the equity is usually pitched.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not because the strategy is wrong or the team is weak — on the evidence, neither is true — but because every hard number turned at once: revenue −10.9% in Q1 2026 (the first decline in nearly three years), net income −57%, operating profit ~−70%, smartphone shipments −19.2% (worst among the top five), connected-devices revenue −24%, and a car division back in the red at ~USD 5,600 per vehicle after two profitable quarters. Free cash flow was already falling 33% before the shock.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *This is not a company-specific problem, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.* Xiaomi's earnings are down because artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory. That means a position in Xiaomi is, mechanically, a **short position on the AI capital-expenditure cycle wearing a consumer-electronics disguise** — the same single shared factor our current regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, with the "memory tax" explicitly identified as the driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23–25 June. The thesis does not resolve on anything Xiaomi does. It resolves when memory supply loosens, which analysts now place at **mid-2027** and which has already been pushed back once. A director must decide whether they want that macro exposure at all before deciding whether they like this company — and must not double-count it against other AI-linked positions.

The second consideration: **the market has not capitulated.** The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy against an average target of HKD 39.52. A drawdown without a sell-side surrender is a falling knife, not a washed-out value setup.

### Economic moat

**Moat type: intangible-brand plus scale-cost, with a thin ecosystem switching-cost layer** (1 billion-plus connected devices, HyperOS, 15,000+ owned stores, and now in-house silicon). It is real — 22 consecutive quarters in the global top three is not luck, and the retail network genuinely lowers customer-acquisition cost across phones, appliances and cars.

**Width: NARROW. Trend: ERODING.** The returns evidence does not support anything wider. Return on invested capital of 8.0% and return on equity of 10.9% are, at best, at the cost of capital — Xiaomi has never earned an excess return, in five years of superb growth. And the memory shock ran the definitive experiment: **a company with a wide moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it** — margins collapsed, and it lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple, who have the balance-sheet depth and the pricing power to absorb the same input inflation. The moat is thin enough that the FY2025 gross margin of 22.3% should be read as a **cyclical peak, not a base** — consistent with our own data showing margins 1.16 standard deviations above their historical peak.

### Secular threat

**Threat: MANAGEABLE. This is a cyclical input shock, not a terminal impairment — and the distinction is the whole investment case.**

The bear temptation is to file Xiaomi under artificial-intelligence displacement. That would be an analytical error. Generative AI is not eating Xiaomi's demand; it is **outbidding Xiaomi for a component**. Nobody is buying fewer phones because of a chatbot. Memory is a notoriously cyclical commodity with a well-documented history of capacity responding to price, and every supplier on earth is now incentivised to build fabs. The demand base is not melting: revenue grew 25% in 2025, the car business is compounding off a genuinely new franchise, and the connected-device installed base is intact.

The honest structural caveats are milder ones: the phone market is mature by management's own admission ("entered a mature phase with overall market showing little growth"), and the car business enters a Chinese price war with real competition. Neither impairs terminal value; both cap it.

**Verdict on the cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — a cyclical trough that is not yet cheap enough.** At ~18x trailing earnings and ~30x trailing free cash flow, on earnings that have already fallen 57% and on a 2026 consensus that still embeds a 550,000-car year that H1 arithmetic contradicts, the shares are **not** priced for terminal decline. They are priced for a recovery that requires a commodity cycle to turn on schedule. The balance sheet (RMB 66.8 billion of net cash) and the buyback mean this is a survivable wait, not a solvency risk. But being early into a cost squeeze that analysts expect to persist through mid-2027, against a consensus that has not yet marked down its car numbers, is not a margin of safety. It is a timing bet on somebody else's capital-expenditure cycle.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not because the strategy is wrong or the team is weak — on the evidence, neither is true — but because every hard number turned at once: revenue −10.9% in Q1 2026 (the first decline in nearly three years), net income −57%, operating profit ~−70%, smartphone shipments −19.2% (worst among the top five), connected-devices revenue −24%, and a car division back in the red at ~USD 5,600 per vehicle after two profitable quarters. Free cash flow was already falling 33% before the shock.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *This is not a company-specific problem, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.* Xiaomi's earnings are down because artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory. That means a position in Xiaomi is, mechanically, a **short position on the AI capital-expenditure cycle wearing a consumer-electronics disguise** — the same single shared factor our current regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, with the "memory tax" explicitly identified as the driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23–25 June. The thesis does not resolve on anything Xiaomi does. It resolves when memory supply loosens, which analysts now place at **mid-2027** and which has already been pushed back once. A director must decide whether they want that macro exposure at all before deciding whether they like this company — and must not double-count it against other AI-linked positions.

The second consideration: **the market has not capitulated.** The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy against an average target of HKD 39.52. A drawdown without a sell-side surrender is a falling knife, not a washed-out value setup.

### Economic moat

**Moat type: intangible-brand plus scale-cost, with a thin ecosystem switching-cost layer** (1 billion-plus connected devices, HyperOS, 15,000+ owned stores, and now in-house silicon). It is real — 22 consecutive quarters in the global top three is not luck, and the retail network genuinely lowers customer-acquisition cost across phones, appliances and cars.

**Width: NARROW. Trend: ERODING.** The returns evidence does not support anything wider. Return on invested capital of 8.0% and return on equity of 10.9% are, at best, at the cost of capital — Xiaomi has never earned an excess return, in five years of superb growth. And the memory shock ran the definitive experiment: **a company with a wide moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it** — margins collapsed, and it lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple, who have the balance-sheet depth and the pricing power to absorb the same input inflation. The moat is thin enough that the FY2025 gross margin of 22.3% should be read as a **cyclical peak, not a base** — consistent with our own data showing margins 1.16 standard deviations above their historical peak.

### Secular threat

**Threat: MANAGEABLE. This is a cyclical input shock, not a terminal impairment — and the distinction is the whole investment case.**

The bear temptation is to file Xiaomi under artificial-intelligence displacement. That would be an analytical error. Generative AI is not eating Xiaomi's demand; it is **outbidding Xiaomi for a component**. Nobody is buying fewer phones because of a chatbot. Memory is a notoriously cyclical commodity with a well-documented history of capacity responding to price, and every supplier on earth is now incentivised to build fabs. The demand base is not melting: revenue grew 25% in 2025, the car business is compounding off a genuinely new franchise, and the connected-device installed base is intact.

The honest structural caveats are milder ones: the phone market is mature by management's own admission ("entered a mature phase with overall market showing little growth"), and the car business enters a Chinese price war with real competition. Neither impairs terminal value; both cap it.

**Verdict on the cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — a cyclical trough that is not yet cheap enough.** At ~18x trailing earnings and ~30x trailing free cash flow, on earnings that have already fallen 57% and on a 2026 consensus that still embeds a 550,000-car year that H1 arithmetic contradicts, the shares are **not** priced for terminal decline. They are priced for a recovery that requires a commodity cycle to turn on schedule. The balance sheet (RMB 66.8 billion of net cash) and the buyback mean this is a survivable wait, not a solvency risk. But being early into a cost squeeze that analysts expect to persist through mid-2027, against a consensus that has not yet marked down its car numbers, is not a margin of safety. It is a timing bet on somebody else's capital-expenditure cycle.

# Forensic Dossier — Xiaomi Corporation (81810.HK / 1810.HK)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-16 · **Transcripts reviewed:** 2024-11-18 (Q3 2024), 2025-03-18 (FY2024), 2025-05-27 (Q1 2025), 2025-08-19 (H1 2025), 2026-03-24 (FY2025) · **Price used:** RMB 23.72 on the renminbi-traded counter (81810.HK); the Hong Kong dollar counter (1810.HK) trades at HKD 27.50.

**Bottom line up front:** Xiaomi's management delivered spectacularly on everything they controlled — smartphone share, premium mix, and a car business built from nothing to 410,000 deliveries in under two years. They were then wrong, repeatedly and with unusual confidence, about the one variable that has since destroyed half the share price: the cost of memory chips. The execution record is genuine. The forecasting record on inputs is broken, and management has now said so themselves.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not so much shift as **compound, then crack**.

**Late 2024 — the three-curve story.** Lu Weibing closes the Q3 2024 call by naming "three growth curves that have already been completed": phones/tablets/wearables, then large home appliances, then vehicles. Revenue was RMB 92.5 billion, up 31%, and the car business had just crossed 100,000 units in 230 days. The tone is a company that has found its formula and is repeating it.

**Early-to-mid 2025 — the hard-tech escalation.** The story widens from "we make good products" to "we are a foundational technology company." The Q1 2025 call is where the ambition peaks: the XRING O1 3-nanometer in-house phone processor, an open-source large language model, and a five-year research budget stepping from RMB 102 billion (2021–2025) to **RMB 200 billion (2026–2030)**. Lu is explicit that financial discipline is subordinate: "today, we are investing without much consideration about cost."

**Late 2025 — the ecosystem/AI layer.** By the FY2025 call (2026-03-24), the emphasis has moved again, to artificial intelligence and robotics: a trillion-parameter model, RMB 60 billion of AI investment over three years, and factory robots. Revenue crossed RMB 400 billion for the first time (RMB 457.3 billion, up 25%), adjusted net profit RMB 39.2 billion, up 44%.

**The quiet crack.** The growth drivers were never dropped — they were overtaken. What changes tone in the FY2025 call is not the strategy but the **admission of forecasting failure on memory**, and one telling aside from Alain Lam: "The second half of 2025 was more challenging [than] the first." The smartphone-and-connected-devices segment grew only 5.4% for the year — the engine that funds everything had already stalled while the AI narrative was being scaled up.

**What is missing from every transcript.** These calls end in March 2026. The Q1 2026 collapse (reported 2026-05-26) is **not in this transcript set** — the story management tells here is one whose central assumption had already failed by the time the market heard about it.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (quarter) | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Gross margin… controllable and stable" for smartphones; memory cost increase "will be a rather slow increase… I don't think the increase will be very drastic" (Q1 2025, 2025-05-27) | Memory contract prices rose **roughly 4–5x year-on-year** for phones and ~10x for TVs; memory is ~60% of the bill of materials on budget devices. Q1 2026 operating profit fell ~70% | **Refuted, decisively.** The single most consequential forecast on the tape, and it was wrong by an order of magnitude |
| "On the cost end, we haven't seen big changes or big change variables" (H1 2025, 2025-08-19) | Two quarters later: revenue −10.9%, net income −57% | **Refuted.** Not a one-off slip — the same reassurance was repeated across quarters |
| "We are fully committed to delivering 550,000 units" of cars in 2026 (FY2025, 2026-03-24) | H1 2026 deliveries **185,055** (+17.2%). Reaching 550,000 needs ~365,000 in H2 — roughly double the first-half rate | **On track to miss**, and the market has not yet been told |
| Revenue and profit at record highs; "high-quality growth" (FY2025) | FY2025 revenue RMB 457.3 billion (+25%), net income RMB 41.6 billion; 5-year EPS CAGR +19.7%, book-value CAGR +16.8% | **Corroborated.** The 2021–2025 record is real and strong |
| Cars: 2024 target 130,000 → 2025 target 300,000 | Delivered ~136,000 then **410,000** — a 37% over-delivery | **Over-delivered.** Elite execution on the thing they controlled |
| Premiumization is working; share of RMB 4,000–6,000 phones tripled in five years (FY2024) | FY2025 premium models 27.1% of China sales, up 3.8 points; global ASP at records | **Corroborated** — but the memory crunch has since forced cancellation of the **Xiaomi 18 Ultra flagship**, which attacks this thesis at its apex |
| "Our strategy… 20% GP margin" and it will hold (Q1 2025) | FY2025 gross margin 22.3% — a record. Then Q1 2026 crushed it | **Held until the input shock, then broke** |
| Cars have reached "economies of scale… quite satisfactory gross margin" (H1 2025) | EV segment made its first profits in Q3/Q4 2025 — then **returned to a RMB 3.1 billion operating loss in Q1 2026**, about **USD 5,600 lost per car** versus ~USD 900 a year earlier | **Corroborated, then reversed** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** Two places. First, returns: for all the record revenue, **return on invested capital is 8.0% and return on equity 10.9%** — this is a company that has never converted its scale into high returns, and the narrative's confidence is not matched by the returns evidence. Second, cash generation: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of RMB 20.8 billion against RMB 41.6 billion of accounting profit, and free cash flow **fell 33% year-on-year** while the story got louder. The car and chip ambitions consume the cash the phone business earns.

**A correction to our own inputs.** The screener's headline numbers on this name are unreliable and should not be used. The scan's "Fair Value 5.79 / Margin of Safety −96%" and "P/FCF 199.1x" cannot be reconciled with the scan's own trailing data: at RMB 23.72, the RMB 613 billion market value against RMB 20.79 billion of trailing free cash flow is about **30x free cash flow**, and trailing earnings of RMB 1.32 per share put the stock at **about 18x**, or ~16x after stripping the net cash. A discounted-cash-flow model that returns a −100% margin of safety on all five methods is registering the car-and-chip capital spending as permanent value destruction, not reading a real signal. The honest bear case here is **not** that the stock is at 199x cash flow — it is that trailing multiples flatter a company whose earnings are actively collapsing.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining** — and the decline is concentrated almost entirely in the last call.

- **Q3 2024 — offensive, expansive.** "We have unlimited potential." "Shopping malls love us." Lu answers a store-count question by raising the target mid-answer.
- **FY2024 — peak conviction.** "The future of Xiaomi is full of infinite possibilities and imagination." Specific, numeric, forward-leaning.
- **Q1 2025 — peak confidence, and the fatal call.** "The key word for results was record high." This is also the call where Lu waves away memory costs and says of the chip programme, "we do not pay much attention to financial targets."
- **H1 2025 — still offensive, with one honest retreat.** Unprompted, Lu corrects his own prior claim on air conditioners: "Let me first correct myself. We are not really #1… There is still a big gap from #1." That is a real green flag; executives protecting a narrative do not volunteer this.
- **FY2025 — the tone breaks.** The language turns defensive and, for the first time, uncertain: "it's very hard for us to quantify that… it is very difficult to foretell early on, **like what we had been able to do before**." And: "In the short term, there may be some pressure on our business." On pricing, the framing shifts from confidence to triage — "we want to maintain our market position," which is the language of defending share, not harvesting it.

The specificity of guidance also inverts. Through 2024–2025 management gave hard numbers freely (store counts, delivery targets, research budgets, share-point goals). On the FY2025 call, asked directly about gross margin and pricing, the answer is qualitative and hedged. When a management team that has been unusually numeric goes vague on the one number that matters, that is information.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** The record splits cleanly in two, and the split is the whole story.

**On outputs — things Xiaomi controls — reliability is High.**

| Guided | Given | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 car deliveries 130,000 | Q3 2024 | ~136,000 ✅ |
| 2025 car deliveries 300,000 | FY2024 | **410,000** ✅ (+37%) |
| 15,000 stores by end-2024, 20,000 by end-2025 | Q3 2024 / FY2024 | ~15,000 confirmed FY2024 ✅ |
| 2025 research spend RMB 30 billion | FY2024 | RMB 33 billion ✅ |
| China share +1 point per year | Repeatedly | Returned to **#1 in China** in Q1 2025, +4.7 points ✅ |

**On inputs and margins — things Xiaomi does not control — reliability is Low.** The memory call was not a near-miss; it was confidently wrong, restated across at least two calls, and it is the direct cause of a 54% drawdown.

**On the reported beat rate.** Our data shows beats in only **1 of the last 3 quarters (33%)**. This does not sit comfortably beside the over-delivery record above, and the reconciliation is instructive: Xiaomi beats on **volume** and misses on **profit**. That is precisely the signature of a company whose costs, not its demand, are out of its control.

**Sandbagging pattern: yes, on volumes, and it has now inverted into its opposite.** Management habitually set delivery targets it could beat (300,000 → 410,000). The 2026 target of 550,000 breaks that habit — with 185,055 delivered in H1, this is the first time in the record that Xiaomi has publicly committed to a number it looks unable to reach. A management team that has trained the market to expect over-delivery is now set up to under-deliver. That reversal is worth more than the target itself.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question they got right and management got wrong.** Citi's Kyna Wong, on the Q1 2025 call, asked directly: "there are other memory vendors who are adjusting their capacity and that will impact the overall supply situation. So, in this regard, will you change your previous view?" Lu declined: "our judgment is that we are quite accurate in our judgment… the impact on Xiaomi will be controllable." **The analyst saw it a full year early. Management dismissed it.** This is the single most important exchange in the transcript set.

**Deflections that recur:**
- **Gross-margin mechanics on cars.** Asked repeatedly (Xu Yingbo, H1 2025) for the cost bridge, the answer is "we do not have much incremental information. Our gross margin is quite good." The EV segment then posted a RMB 3.1 billion loss.
- **Chip economics.** Asked how a self-designed processor affects margins, Lu answers: "this is too early to talk about that… right now, we do not pay much attention to financial targets." Four-plus years and RMB 13.5 billion in, "too early" is a non-answer.
- **Monetizing AI.** Asked point-blank when the models generate revenue (FY2025), the answer is "commercialization is too early to talk about." Xiaomi is spending RMB 60 billion over three years against an explicitly undefined return.
- **Robotics.** "I won't comment on that… I haven't seen very clear timetable for commercial closed loop."

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing.** Nobody on these calls asks the question that now decides the stock: *what happens to a business where 60% of the bill of materials on your volume products is a commodity you do not make, whose price just went up fivefold?* Management's answer, implicitly, is to raise prices and hope — "product innovation, technological capability, these are important, even though memory is hiking in prices."

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The memory call (Q1 2025, restated H1 2025).** Confidently wrong on the one input that mattered, after being handed the question by an analyst.

🔴 **Explicit loss of forecasting ability (FY2025).** "It is very difficult to foretell early on, like what we had been able to do before" — a company that has lost visibility into its own cost base.

🔴 **A 550,000-car commitment that H1 arithmetic (185,055) contradicts.** The first live guidance in the record that looks unreachable.

🔴 **Returns never followed scale.** ROIC 8.0% after five years of 20%+ growth. Xiaomi buys share and volume; it has not bought pricing power — and the memory shock proved it, because a company with real pricing power passes a cost shock through.

🔴 **Free cash flow down 33% while the investment budget steps up** to RMB 40 billion (2026) and RMB 200 billion (2026–2030). The commitments are structural and were sized in a fatter-margin world.

🔴 **Flagship cancellation.** The Xiaomi 18 Ultra was scrapped over memory costs — the premiumization thesis losing its halo product is a strategic casualty, not a cost line.

🔴 **Governance tension (July 2026, outside the transcripts).** Caixin reports staff reductions across divisions since March toward a preliminary ~30% target; the company calls them routine. Either the report is wrong or the public research-spending guidance is not the whole picture. Both cannot be comfortably true.

🟢 **Unprompted self-correction (H1 2025).** "Let me first correct myself. We are not really #1." Rare, and it earns real credibility.

🟢 **The car business is not a slide — it is 410,000 units** in year two, against a 300,000 target, with a Nürburgring record and 240,000 pre-orders for the YU7 in 18 hours. Whatever else is wrong, this team ships.

🟢 **Genuine net cash: RMB 66.8 billion** (RMB 102.05 billion cash against RMB 35.25 billion of debt, at 2026-03-31). This company does not face a solvency question; it faces an earnings question.

🟢 **Capital returned while the stock fell.** ~399.6 million Class B shares repurchased for ~HKD 14.6 billion under the prior programme, a new **HKD 20 billion** authorisation effective 2026-06-02, and an automatic HKD 4 billion tranche from 2026-06-19. They are buying their own shares into the drawdown.

🟢 **In-house silicon is real.** A shipping 3-nanometer processor puts Xiaomi in a category with Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and MediaTek. It is the one genuinely moat-deepening investment on the tape.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrates with the funding need.** Track the load-bearing noun by call: *stores and share* (2024) → *chips* (Q1 2025) → *AI and robots* (FY2025). Each new frontier arrives with a bigger number attached (RMB 50 billion for chips → RMB 60 billion for AI → RMB 200 billion for research). The pattern is a company that answers a maturing core business by opening a new frontier. Sometimes that is visionary. It is also, mechanically, how returns on capital stay at 8%.

**"Scale and profit" quietly became "maintain our market position."** In FY2024 Lu described a philosophy shift from "scale first" to "long-term sustainable high-quality growth." By FY2025, under cost pressure, the revealed priority is share: "we want to maintain our market position. That is very important to us." The 2022-era philosophy did not survive its first real test.

**A new voice, less certainty.** The FY2025 call is partly answered by an "Unknown Executive" rather than the usual Lu/Lam pairing, and it is that voice which delivers the memory-cost capitulation. Note also the interpreter's currency errors throughout the earlier calls ("JPY365.9 billion" for RMB) — a transcription artifact, not a signal, but a reason to trust the reported financials over the transcript text.

**The tell they did not intend.** Lu's own cost taxonomy on the FY2025 call — memory hurts "smartphone, notebook and also tablets" most, "less so for smart cars… and even less so for IoT" — is management ranking its own segments by vulnerability. It confirms that the profit engine (phones) is the most exposed part, and that the car business, the growth story, is the *shelter*. That is the opposite of how the equity is usually pitched.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not because the strategy is wrong or the team is weak — on the evidence, neither is true — but because every hard number turned at once: revenue −10.9% in Q1 2026 (the first decline in nearly three years), net income −57%, operating profit ~−70%, smartphone shipments −19.2% (worst among the top five), connected-devices revenue −24%, and a car division back in the red at ~USD 5,600 per vehicle after two profitable quarters. Free cash flow was already falling 33% before the shock.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *This is not a company-specific problem, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.* Xiaomi's earnings are down because artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory. That means a position in Xiaomi is, mechanically, a **short position on the AI capital-expenditure cycle wearing a consumer-electronics disguise** — the same single shared factor our current regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, with the "memory tax" explicitly identified as the driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23–25 June. The thesis does not resolve on anything Xiaomi does. It resolves when memory supply loosens, which analysts now place at **mid-2027** and which has already been pushed back once. A director must decide whether they want that macro exposure at all before deciding whether they like this company — and must not double-count it against other AI-linked positions.

The second consideration: **the market has not capitulated.** The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy against an average target of HKD 39.52. A drawdown without a sell-side surrender is a falling knife, not a washed-out value setup.

### Economic moat

**Moat type: intangible-brand plus scale-cost, with a thin ecosystem switching-cost layer** (1 billion-plus connected devices, HyperOS, 15,000+ owned stores, and now in-house silicon). It is real — 22 consecutive quarters in the global top three is not luck, and the retail network genuinely lowers customer-acquisition cost across phones, appliances and cars.

**Width: NARROW. Trend: ERODING.** The returns evidence does not support anything wider. Return on invested capital of 8.0% and return on equity of 10.9% are, at best, at the cost of capital — Xiaomi has never earned an excess return, in five years of superb growth. And the memory shock ran the definitive experiment: **a company with a wide moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it** — margins collapsed, and it lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple, who have the balance-sheet depth and the pricing power to absorb the same input inflation. The moat is thin enough that the FY2025 gross margin of 22.3% should be read as a **cyclical peak, not a base** — consistent with our own data showing margins 1.16 standard deviations above their historical peak.

### Secular threat

**Threat: MANAGEABLE. This is a cyclical input shock, not a terminal impairment — and the distinction is the whole investment case.**

The bear temptation is to file Xiaomi under artificial-intelligence displacement. That would be an analytical error. Generative AI is not eating Xiaomi's demand; it is **outbidding Xiaomi for a component**. Nobody is buying fewer phones because of a chatbot. Memory is a notoriously cyclical commodity with a well-documented history of capacity responding to price, and every supplier on earth is now incentivised to build fabs. The demand base is not melting: revenue grew 25% in 2025, the car business is compounding off a genuinely new franchise, and the connected-device installed base is intact.

The honest structural caveats are milder ones: the phone market is mature by management's own admission ("entered a mature phase with overall market showing little growth"), and the car business enters a Chinese price war with real competition. Neither impairs terminal value; both cap it.

**Verdict on the cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — a cyclical trough that is not yet cheap enough.** At ~18x trailing earnings and ~30x trailing free cash flow, on earnings that have already fallen 57% and on a 2026 consensus that still embeds a 550,000-car year that H1 arithmetic contradicts, the shares are **not** priced for terminal decline. They are priced for a recovery that requires a commodity cycle to turn on schedule. The balance sheet (RMB 66.8 billion of net cash) and the buyback mean this is a survivable wait, not a solvency risk. But being early into a cost squeeze that analysts expect to persist through mid-2027, against a consensus that has not yet marked down its car numbers, is not a margin of safety. It is a timing bet on somebody else's capital-expenditure cycle.

bull_thesis: The bull case is that this is a great operator being punished for a commodity price it does not control, and that the commodity will mean-revert. Xiaomi's problem is precise and external: artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory chips, pushing DRAM and NAND contract prices to roughly four to five times year-ago levels. Memory is the most reliably cyclical input in electronics; every supplier now has maximum incentive to add capacity, and when the cycle turns, the earnings that vanished come back roughly as fast as they left. Underneath the squeeze the franchise is intact and, in places, still compounding. Full-year 2025 revenue reached RMB 457.3 billion, up 25%, with adjusted net profit of RMB 39.2 billion, up 44%. The car business went from nothing to 410,000 deliveries in 2025 against a 300,000 target — a 37% over-delivery — and 185,055 more in the first half of 2026. Premium phones reached 27.1% of China sales, and the company shipped its own 3-nanometer processor, putting it in a club with Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and MediaTek. Management has committed RMB 200 billion of research spending for 2026-2030 and RMB 60 billion to artificial intelligence over three years, funded from a genuine net cash position of RMB 66.8 billion (RMB 102.05 billion of cash against RMB 35.25 billion of debt at 31 March 2026). This is a balance sheet that can wait out a cost cycle, and management is using it: about 399.6 million Class B shares were repurchased for roughly HKD 14.6 billion under the prior programme, a fresh HKD 20 billion authorisation took effect on 2 June 2026, and an automatic HKD 4 billion tranche began on 19 June 2026 — the company is buying its own stock into the drawdown. The valuation is not demanding on any normalised measure: at RMB 23.72 the shares trade at about 18 times trailing earnings of RMB 1.32 per share, or roughly 16 times after stripping the RMB 2.57 per share of net cash. If memory normalises by mid-2027 and earnings return to the RMB 1.50-1.70 range, a 16-18 times multiple puts the shares meaningfully higher, with the car business and any eventual artificial-intelligence monetisation as unpaid options on top. The conditions this case requires: memory supply must actually loosen on roughly the expected schedule; Xiaomi must hold its share position through the squeeze rather than buy it back with permanent margin concessions; and the car business must return to the profitability it briefly demonstrated in the third and fourth quarters of 2025.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that the memory squeeze is not the problem but the diagnostic — it revealed that Xiaomi has no pricing power, and the market has not finished repricing that discovery. A company with a real moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it, and lost the volume anyway: first-quarter 2026 shipments fell 19.2% to 33.8 million units, the steepest decline among the top five global brands, while Samsung and Apple — who face the identical input inflation with deeper balance sheets and real pricing power — took share. Operating profit fell about 70%. The connected-devices segment fell 24% to RMB 24.7 billion as Chinese trade-in subsidies faded, removing a prop that had flattered 2025. The car business, the entire growth story, returned to a RMB 3.1 billion operating loss on 20.1% gross margin (down from 23.2%) — about USD 5,600 lost per vehicle versus roughly USD 900 a year earlier — after only two profitable quarters. The returns evidence says this was always the case: return on invested capital is 8.0% and return on equity 10.9% after five years of 20%-plus growth. Xiaomi has never earned an excess return on capital; it buys share and volume. That reframes the 22.3% gross margin of 2025 as a cyclical peak rather than a base — consistent with margins sitting 1.16 standard deviations above their own historical peak — and it means normalised earnings may be materially below what the bull case extrapolates. Management's credibility on this specific variable is spent. On the first-quarter 2025 call, handed the question directly by Citi's analyst, Lu Weibing said the memory cost increase would be 'a rather slow increase', that 'I do not think the increase will be very drastic', and that smartphone gross margin was 'controllable and stable'. He repeated the reassurance in August 2025: 'on the cost end, we have not seen big changes or big change variables.' By the March 2026 call the same team conceded 'it is very difficult to foretell early on, like what we had been able to do before.' A live commitment now rests on that broken forecasting: management said in March 2026 it was 'fully committed to delivering 550,000' cars in 2026, but 185,055 units in the first half means the second half must nearly double — the first unreachable target in the company's public record, from a team that had trained the market to expect over-delivery. Strategically, the squeeze is already destroying franchise value, not just earnings: the flagship Xiaomi 18 Ultra was cancelled outright over memory costs, decapitating the premiumisation thesis at its apex, and analysts expect the constraint to persist through mid-2027. Meanwhile the cost base is committed and rising — RMB 40 billion of research spending guided for 2026 into collapsing profits, with Caixin reporting staff cuts across divisions since March toward a preliminary ~30% target that the company calls routine. Free cash flow had already fallen 33% before the shock. What confirms the bear: the second-quarter results due in late August 2026 showing continued margin compression, and the 550,000 car target being walked back. The deepest problem is that none of this resolves on anything Xiaomi does — it resolves when memory loosens, a date owned by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, already pushed out once.
consensus_delta: For a name tagged deep value, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with stable or growing earnings power. Here the answer is the opposite of the one the tag implies, and that is the whole finding: the market has not capitulated at all. The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high above HKD 61, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy, against an average twelve-month target of HKD 39.52 — roughly 44% above the HKD 27.50 at which the Hong Kong dollar counter trades. Only three say sell. A 54% drawdown with an intact buy consensus is a falling knife, not a fear-print. So where we disagree with the market is not the direction the street is looking — it is that the street has not yet marked its own model. Three specific consensus assumptions are factually strained. First, that average target embeds a 550,000-car year, because that is the number management committed to on 24 March 2026 and no one has been told otherwise. First-half deliveries of 185,055 require the second half to deliver about 365,000 — nearly double the run rate — and Jefferies' Edison Lee (Underperform, HKD 25.49, cut from Hold) and a 14 July sell-side downgrade citing exactly this are so far the only voices marking it. The target is anchored to a number that will be revised. Second, consensus treats the memory squeeze as a one-to-two-quarter dent. The dated evidence says otherwise: DRAM and NAND at four to five times year-ago levels, contract prices up roughly fivefold for phones and tenfold for televisions, memory at ~60% of budget-device bill of materials, and analysts now placing normalisation at mid-2027 — a date already pushed out once. That is three to four more quarters of compression, not one. Third, and most subtly, the street models this as a margin dent while treating market share as stable. It is not: shipments fell 19.2% in the first quarter, the worst of the top five, and reporting on 15 July confirms share slipping to Samsung and Apple. Xiaomi is paying the cost shock and losing the volume — the worst of both. Our honest counter-position: we are not more bearish than the price. We are more bearish than the consensus that sits behind the price, and the gap between HKD 39.52 and reality has to close before this becomes interesting.
forcing_function: There is no hard date, and that is the disqualifying feature. The re-rating driver is memory normalisation, and it has all four marks of a soft, non-binding catalyst: it is owned by third parties (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron), it is undated, it is a commodity cycle rather than a contractual event, and it has already been pushed out once — from an implied second-half-2026 recovery to analyst expectations now clustered at mid-2027. There is no contract, no deal term and no scheduled decision that pays anybody anything. What the calendar actually offers, in order: the interim results in late August 2026, which are a dated event but a negatively-skewed one — the most likely content is another compressed quarter plus the walk-back of the 550,000-car target, which forces a re-rating downward, not up. Beyond that, the electric-vehicle business is scheduled to enter Europe in 2027, and management has said artificial-intelligence commercialisation is 'too early to talk about' — an explicit statement that the option has no exercise date. The HKD 20 billion buyback is the closest thing to a company-controlled catalyst, and it has already fired: it was authorised on 2 June 2026, the automatic tranche began 19 June, and the stock made new lows anyway. A catalyst that has run without effect is spent. The honest forcing function for this name is a memory spot-price roll-over confirmed by supplier capacity guidance, plus a reset car target that consensus has actually marked to — and the right posture is to watch for both rather than to pay for them in advance.
valley_of_death: For a deep-value name the question is whether an event kills the thesis before the discount converges. There is no solvency question here — RMB 66.8 billion of net cash and no maturity wall mean Xiaomi cannot be forced into anything. The risk is entirely that the next three to nine months keep resetting earnings downward while the memory clock runs. Four dated things sit in that window. First and largest, the second-quarter and interim results due in late August 2026 (our data shows the next report about 41 days out): the memory squeeze was in full effect for the whole quarter, the connected-devices business laps the expiry of Chinese trade-in subsidies that flattered 2025, and the car division enters with unit economics of about USD 5,600 lost per vehicle. There is no mechanism by which that print is good. Second, the 550,000-car target has to be walked back, most likely at those same interim results or at the third quarter — the first guidance cut in this management's public record, from a team that had trained the market on over-delivery. That is a credibility event, not just a numbers event. Third, the premium mix deteriorates on a cancelled product: the Xiaomi 18 Ultra was scrapped over memory costs, so the second half loses its halo flagship while the Redmi Note 17 (launched 14 July) and the SkyNomad SUV (unveiled 14 July) ship into an inflated bill of materials. Fourth, the cost base is committed and moving the wrong way — RMB 40 billion of research spending guided for 2026 and RMB 60 billion of artificial-intelligence investment over three years, sized in a fatter-margin world, against free cash flow that had already fallen 33% before the shock. The Caixin report of staff cuts since March toward a preliminary ~30% target, which the company calls routine, suggests the internal view of the squeeze is more severe than the external guidance. And the macro overlay cuts against the entry: our regime read places a hawkish Fed under Warsh with roughly 77% odds of a hike by December, which is a headwind for a long-duration Chinese growth multiple. The thesis does not die in this window. It just gets cheaper, and the cheapness that matters arrives after the guidance cut, not before it.
positioning_washout: The candid answer is that there is no washout here, and its absence is a large part of the case for waiting. The mechanics that normally force selling are all missing. There is no dividend to cut, so there is no yield-focused holder base to be mechanically ejected. There is no covenant, no maturity and no rating trigger, because the company sits on RMB 66.8 billion of net cash. Xiaomi is a major constituent of the Hang Seng, Hang Seng China Enterprises and Hang Seng Tech indices, so a large slice of the register is passive and will not sell on fundamentals — it will only sell if index weights fall, which is a lagging consequence of a lower price rather than a cause of one. And the single largest identifiable flow is pointing the other way: the company itself is a price-insensitive buyer, with roughly HKD 14.6 billion of Class B shares already repurchased under the prior programme, a HKD 20 billion authorisation live from 2 June 2026 and an automatic HKD 4 billion tranche running since 19 June 2026. That is support, not pressure — though at roughly 3% of market value it is a cushion, not a floor, and it has manifestly not stopped the stock from making new lows. What has not happened yet is the real washout: the holder base is still substantially made of growth and momentum money that owns this as a Chinese artificial-intelligence and electric-vehicle winner. The label is in the process of inverting to artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure victim, and that re-labelling — not a margin call — is what would force the rotation. It typically completes on a guidance cut, which is exactly what the 550,000-car target sets up for late August. One execution note specific to this listing: the renminbi counter (81810.HK) traded about 310,000 shares against 319 million on the Hong Kong dollar counter (1810.HK) in the same session. This counter is thin to the point that position size is constrained regardless of the view, and it prices at roughly a 5% discount to the Hong Kong dollar counter's currency-adjusted level — a real consideration for entry and, more importantly, for exit.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now — a good company, a real drawdown, and the wrong trade at this price. Xiaomi is not broken. The 2021-2025 record is genuine (revenue compounding to RMB 457.3 billion in 2025, up 25%; a car business from zero to 410,000 deliveries against a 300,000 target; a shipping in-house 3-nanometer processor; RMB 66.8 billion of net cash), and the thing hurting it is external and cyclical: artificial-intelligence data centres outbidding phone makers for memory, with DRAM and NAND at four to five times year-ago levels. That is a cost shock, not the death of demand, which is why we call the structural threat manageable rather than terminal and refuse to file this under artificial-intelligence displacement. Nobody buys fewer phones because of a chatbot. But three things stop this from being a buy, and they compound. First, the arithmetic. Our parts-based fair value is about RMB 26.00 against a live RMB 23.72 — roughly 10% of upside — while the adverse case sits at RMB 15.50, about 35% below. Risking three to make one is not value investing, it is hope with a spreadsheet. The shares fell 54% and are still only fair. Second, the market has not capitulated. Twenty-three of thirty analysts still say buy, with an average target of HKD 39.52 against HKD 27.50 — a target that embeds a 550,000-car year that first-half deliveries of 185,055 have already made unreachable. Deep value requires the street to have surrendered; here the street has not yet marked its own model, so the next revisions are still downward. Third, and decisive under the current regime: this thesis resolves on one shared macro factor that Xiaomi does not control. Owning it is a short position on the artificial-intelligence capital-expenditure cycle in consumer-electronics clothing — the same factor our regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, and the identified driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23-25 June. The regime rewards hard-dated catalysts and structural special situations in thinly-covered lanes, and penalises theses that hinge on a single shared driver arriving on schedule. This name is the mirror image of what the regime wants: thirty analysts, no hard date, and a recovery clock owned by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron that has already slipped once, to mid-2027. The moat read confirms the discipline. The memory shock ran the experiment for us: a wide-moat company passes a cost shock to customers, and Xiaomi ate it and lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple. Eight percent return on invested capital after five years of superb growth says this was always a narrow moat with an eroding trend, and that the record 22.3% gross margin of 2025 was a cyclical peak, not a base. On valuation alone, ignoring every catalyst and the regime entirely, the value case rates a 2 — about 10% below our own fair value, on collapsing earnings and a return on capital that has never exceeded its cost, is roughly fair, not cheap. What would change this: a memory spot-price roll-over confirmed by supplier capacity guidance, a reset car target that consensus has actually marked to, and a price closer to RMB 18-19 where the adverse case is covered and the recovery is free. The late-August interim results are the event to watch — most likely another compressed quarter plus the first guidance cut in this management's record. That is the flush worth waiting for. Buy the wash-out, not the fall.
