interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Xiaomi Corporation (81810.HK / 1810.HK)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-16 · **Transcripts reviewed:** 2024-11-18 (Q3 2024), 2025-03-18 (FY2024), 2025-05-27 (Q1 2025), 2025-08-19 (H1 2025), 2026-03-24 (FY2025) · **Price used:** RMB 23.72 on the renminbi-traded counter (81810.HK); the Hong Kong dollar counter (1810.HK) trades at HKD 27.50.

**Bottom line up front:** Xiaomi's management delivered spectacularly on everything they controlled — smartphone share, premium mix, and a car business built from nothing to 410,000 deliveries in under two years. They were then wrong, repeatedly and with unusual confidence, about the one variable that has since destroyed half the share price: the cost of memory chips. The execution record is genuine. The forecasting record on inputs is broken, and management has now said so themselves.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not so much shift as **compound, then crack**.

**Late 2024 — the three-curve story.** Lu Weibing closes the Q3 2024 call by naming "three growth curves that have already been completed": phones/tablets/wearables, then large home appliances, then vehicles. Revenue was RMB 92.5 billion, up 31%, and the car business had just crossed 100,000 units in 230 days. The tone is a company that has found its formula and is repeating it.

**Early-to-mid 2025 — the hard-tech escalation.** The story widens from "we make good products" to "we are a foundational technology company." The Q1 2025 call is where the ambition peaks: the XRING O1 3-nanometer in-house phone processor, an open-source large language model, and a five-year research budget stepping from RMB 102 billion (2021–2025) to **RMB 200 billion (2026–2030)**. Lu is explicit that financial discipline is subordinate: "today, we are investing without much consideration about cost."

**Late 2025 — the ecosystem/AI layer.** By the FY2025 call (2026-03-24), the emphasis has moved again, to artificial intelligence and robotics: a trillion-parameter model, RMB 60 billion of AI investment over three years, and factory robots. Revenue crossed RMB 400 billion for the first time (RMB 457.3 billion, up 25%), adjusted net profit RMB 39.2 billion, up 44%.

**The quiet crack.** The growth drivers were never dropped — they were overtaken. What changes tone in the FY2025 call is not the strategy but the **admission of forecasting failure on memory**, and one telling aside from Alain Lam: "The second half of 2025 was more challenging [than] the first." The smartphone-and-connected-devices segment grew only 5.4% for the year — the engine that funds everything had already stalled while the AI narrative was being scaled up.

**What is missing from every transcript.** These calls end in March 2026. The Q1 2026 collapse (reported 2026-05-26) is **not in this transcript set** — the story management tells here is one whose central assumption had already failed by the time the market heard about it.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (quarter) | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Gross margin… controllable and stable" for smartphones; memory cost increase "will be a rather slow increase… I don't think the increase will be very drastic" (Q1 2025, 2025-05-27) | Memory contract prices rose **roughly 4–5x year-on-year** for phones and ~10x for TVs; memory is ~60% of the bill of materials on budget devices. Q1 2026 operating profit fell ~70% | **Refuted, decisively.** The single most consequential forecast on the tape, and it was wrong by an order of magnitude |
| "On the cost end, we haven't seen big changes or big change variables" (H1 2025, 2025-08-19) | Two quarters later: revenue −10.9%, net income −57% | **Refuted.** Not a one-off slip — the same reassurance was repeated across quarters |
| "We are fully committed to delivering 550,000 units" of cars in 2026 (FY2025, 2026-03-24) | H1 2026 deliveries **185,055** (+17.2%). Reaching 550,000 needs ~365,000 in H2 — roughly double the first-half rate | **On track to miss**, and the market has not yet been told |
| Revenue and profit at record highs; "high-quality growth" (FY2025) | FY2025 revenue RMB 457.3 billion (+25%), net income RMB 41.6 billion; 5-year EPS CAGR +19.7%, book-value CAGR +16.8% | **Corroborated.** The 2021–2025 record is real and strong |
| Cars: 2024 target 130,000 → 2025 target 300,000 | Delivered ~136,000 then **410,000** — a 37% over-delivery | **Over-delivered.** Elite execution on the thing they controlled |
| Premiumization is working; share of RMB 4,000–6,000 phones tripled in five years (FY2024) | FY2025 premium models 27.1% of China sales, up 3.8 points; global ASP at records | **Corroborated** — but the memory crunch has since forced cancellation of the **Xiaomi 18 Ultra flagship**, which attacks this thesis at its apex |
| "Our strategy… 20% GP margin" and it will hold (Q1 2025) | FY2025 gross margin 22.3% — a record. Then Q1 2026 crushed it | **Held until the input shock, then broke** |
| Cars have reached "economies of scale… quite satisfactory gross margin" (H1 2025) | EV segment made its first profits in Q3/Q4 2025 — then **returned to a RMB 3.1 billion operating loss in Q1 2026**, about **USD 5,600 lost per car** versus ~USD 900 a year earlier | **Corroborated, then reversed** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** Two places. First, returns: for all the record revenue, **return on invested capital is 8.0% and return on equity 10.9%** — this is a company that has never converted its scale into high returns, and the narrative's confidence is not matched by the returns evidence. Second, cash generation: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of RMB 20.8 billion against RMB 41.6 billion of accounting profit, and free cash flow **fell 33% year-on-year** while the story got louder. The car and chip ambitions consume the cash the phone business earns.

**A correction to our own inputs.** The screener's headline numbers on this name are unreliable and should not be used. The scan's "Fair Value 5.79 / Margin of Safety −96%" and "P/FCF 199.1x" cannot be reconciled with the scan's own trailing data: at RMB 23.72, the RMB 613 billion market value against RMB 20.79 billion of trailing free cash flow is about **30x free cash flow**, and trailing earnings of RMB 1.32 per share put the stock at **about 18x**, or ~16x after stripping the net cash. A discounted-cash-flow model that returns a −100% margin of safety on all five methods is registering the car-and-chip capital spending as permanent value destruction, not reading a real signal. The honest bear case here is **not** that the stock is at 199x cash flow — it is that trailing multiples flatter a company whose earnings are actively collapsing.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining** — and the decline is concentrated almost entirely in the last call.

- **Q3 2024 — offensive, expansive.** "We have unlimited potential." "Shopping malls love us." Lu answers a store-count question by raising the target mid-answer.
- **FY2024 — peak conviction.** "The future of Xiaomi is full of infinite possibilities and imagination." Specific, numeric, forward-leaning.
- **Q1 2025 — peak confidence, and the fatal call.** "The key word for results was record high." This is also the call where Lu waves away memory costs and says of the chip programme, "we do not pay much attention to financial targets."
- **H1 2025 — still offensive, with one honest retreat.** Unprompted, Lu corrects his own prior claim on air conditioners: "Let me first correct myself. We are not really #1… There is still a big gap from #1." That is a real green flag; executives protecting a narrative do not volunteer this.
- **FY2025 — the tone breaks.** The language turns defensive and, for the first time, uncertain: "it's very hard for us to quantify that… it is very difficult to foretell early on, **like what we had been able to do before**." And: "In the short term, there may be some pressure on our business." On pricing, the framing shifts from confidence to triage — "we want to maintain our market position," which is the language of defending share, not harvesting it.

The specificity of guidance also inverts. Through 2024–2025 management gave hard numbers freely (store counts, delivery targets, research budgets, share-point goals). On the FY2025 call, asked directly about gross margin and pricing, the answer is qualitative and hedged. When a management team that has been unusually numeric goes vague on the one number that matters, that is information.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.** The record splits cleanly in two, and the split is the whole story.

**On outputs — things Xiaomi controls — reliability is High.**

| Guided | Given | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 car deliveries 130,000 | Q3 2024 | ~136,000 ✅ |
| 2025 car deliveries 300,000 | FY2024 | **410,000** ✅ (+37%) |
| 15,000 stores by end-2024, 20,000 by end-2025 | Q3 2024 / FY2024 | ~15,000 confirmed FY2024 ✅ |
| 2025 research spend RMB 30 billion | FY2024 | RMB 33 billion ✅ |
| China share +1 point per year | Repeatedly | Returned to **#1 in China** in Q1 2025, +4.7 points ✅ |

**On inputs and margins — things Xiaomi does not control — reliability is Low.** The memory call was not a near-miss; it was confidently wrong, restated across at least two calls, and it is the direct cause of a 54% drawdown.

**On the reported beat rate.** Our data shows beats in only **1 of the last 3 quarters (33%)**. This does not sit comfortably beside the over-delivery record above, and the reconciliation is instructive: Xiaomi beats on **volume** and misses on **profit**. That is precisely the signature of a company whose costs, not its demand, are out of its control.

**Sandbagging pattern: yes, on volumes, and it has now inverted into its opposite.** Management habitually set delivery targets it could beat (300,000 → 410,000). The 2026 target of 550,000 breaks that habit — with 185,055 delivered in H1, this is the first time in the record that Xiaomi has publicly committed to a number it looks unable to reach. A management team that has trained the market to expect over-delivery is now set up to under-deliver. That reversal is worth more than the target itself.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question they got right and management got wrong.** Citi's Kyna Wong, on the Q1 2025 call, asked directly: "there are other memory vendors who are adjusting their capacity and that will impact the overall supply situation. So, in this regard, will you change your previous view?" Lu declined: "our judgment is that we are quite accurate in our judgment… the impact on Xiaomi will be controllable." **The analyst saw it a full year early. Management dismissed it.** This is the single most important exchange in the transcript set.

**Deflections that recur:**
- **Gross-margin mechanics on cars.** Asked repeatedly (Xu Yingbo, H1 2025) for the cost bridge, the answer is "we do not have much incremental information. Our gross margin is quite good." The EV segment then posted a RMB 3.1 billion loss.
- **Chip economics.** Asked how a self-designed processor affects margins, Lu answers: "this is too early to talk about that… right now, we do not pay much attention to financial targets." Four-plus years and RMB 13.5 billion in, "too early" is a non-answer.
- **Monetizing AI.** Asked point-blank when the models generate revenue (FY2025), the answer is "commercialization is too early to talk about." Xiaomi is spending RMB 60 billion over three years against an explicitly undefined return.
- **Robotics.** "I won't comment on that… I haven't seen very clear timetable for commercial closed loop."

They are buying their own shares into the drawdown.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrates with the funding need.** Track the load-bearing noun by call: *stores and share* (2024) → *chips* (Q1 2025) → *AI and robots* (FY2025). Each new frontier arrives with a bigger number attached (RMB 50 billion for chips → RMB 60 billion for AI → RMB 200 billion for research). The pattern is a company that answers a maturing core business by opening a new frontier. Sometimes that is visionary. It is also, mechanically, how returns on capital stay at 8%.

**"Scale and profit" quietly became "maintain our market position."** In FY2024 Lu described a philosophy shift from "scale first" to "long-term sustainable high-quality growth." By FY2025, under cost pressure, the revealed priority is share: "we want to maintain our market position. That is very important to us." The 2022-era philosophy did not survive its first real test.

**A new voice, less certainty.** The FY2025 call is partly answered by an "Unknown Executive" rather than the usual Lu/Lam pairing, and it is that voice which delivers the memory-cost capitulation. Note also the interpreter's currency errors throughout the earlier calls ("JPY365.9 billion" for RMB) — a transcription artifact, not a signal, but a reason to trust the reported financials over the transcript text.

**The tell they did not intend.** Lu's own cost taxonomy on the FY2025 call — memory hurts "smartphone, notebook and also tablets" most, "less so for smart cars… and even less so for IoT" — is management ranking its own segments by vulnerability. It confirms that the profit engine (phones) is the most exposed part, and that the car business, the growth story, is the *shelter*. That is the opposite of how the equity is usually pitched.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not because the strategy is wrong or the team is weak — on the evidence, neither is true — but because every hard number turned at once: revenue −10.9% in Q1 2026 (the first decline in nearly three years), net income −57%, operating profit ~−70%, smartphone shipments −19.2% (worst among the top five), connected-devices revenue −24%, and a car division back in the red at ~USD 5,600 per vehicle after two profitable quarters. Free cash flow was already falling 33% before the shock.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *This is not a company-specific problem, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.* Xiaomi's earnings are down because artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory. That means a position in Xiaomi is, mechanically, a **short position on the AI capital-expenditure cycle wearing a consumer-electronics disguise** — the same single shared factor our current regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, with the "memory tax" explicitly identified as the driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23–25 June. The thesis does not resolve on anything Xiaomi does. It resolves when memory supply loosens, which analysts now place at **mid-2027** and which has already been pushed back once. A director must decide whether they want that macro exposure at all before deciding whether they like this company — and must not double-count it against other AI-linked positions.

The second consideration: **the market has not capitulated.** The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy against an average target of HKD 39.52. A drawdown without a sell-side surrender is a falling knife, not a washed-out value setup.

### Economic moat

**Moat type: intangible-brand plus scale-cost, with a thin ecosystem switching-cost layer** (1 billion-plus connected devices, HyperOS, 15,000+ owned stores, and now in-house silicon). It is real — 22 consecutive quarters in the global top three is not luck, and the retail network genuinely lowers customer-acquisition cost across phones, appliances and cars.

**Width: NARROW. Trend: ERODING.** The returns evidence does not support anything wider. Return on invested capital of 8.0% and return on equity of 10.9% are, at best, at the cost of capital — Xiaomi has never earned an excess return, in five years of superb growth. And the memory shock ran the definitive experiment: **a company with a wide moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it** — margins collapsed, and it lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple, who have the balance-sheet depth and the pricing power to absorb the same input inflation. The moat is thin enough that the FY2025 gross margin of 22.3% should be read as a **cyclical peak, not a base** — consistent with our own data showing margins 1.16 standard deviations above their historical peak.

### Secular threat

**Threat: MANAGEABLE. This is a cyclical input shock, not a terminal impairment — and the distinction is the whole investment case.**

The bear temptation is to file Xiaomi under artificial-intelligence displacement. That would be an analytical error. Generative AI is not eating Xiaomi's demand; it is **outbidding Xiaomi for a component**. Nobody is buying fewer phones because of a chatbot. Memory is a notoriously cyclical commodity with a well-documented history of capacity responding to price, and every supplier on earth is now incentivised to build fabs. The demand base is not melting: revenue grew 25% in 2025, the car business is compounding off a genuinely new franchise, and the connected-device installed base is intact.

The honest structural caveats are milder ones: the phone market is mature by management's own admission ("entered a mature phase with overall market showing little growth"), and the car business enters a Chinese price war with real competition. Neither impairs terminal value; both cap it.

**Verdict on the cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — a cyclical trough that is not yet cheap enough.** At ~18x trailing earnings and ~30x trailing free cash flow, on earnings that have already fallen 57% and on a 2026 consensus that still embeds a 550,000-car year that H1 arithmetic contradicts, the shares are **not** priced for terminal decline. They are priced for a recovery that requires a commodity cycle to turn on schedule. The balance sheet (RMB 66.8 billion of net cash) and the buyback mean this is a survivable wait, not a solvency risk. But being early into a cost squeeze that analysts expect to persist through mid-2027, against a consensus that has not yet marked down its car numbers, is not a margin of safety. It is a timing bet on somebody else's capital-expenditure cycle.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrates with the funding need.** Track the load-bearing noun by call: *stores and share* (2024) → *chips* (Q1 2025) → *AI and robots* (FY2025). Each new frontier arrives with a bigger number attached (RMB 50 billion for chips → RMB 60 billion for AI → RMB 200 billion for research). The pattern is a company that answers a maturing core business by opening a new frontier. Sometimes that is visionary. It is also, mechanically, how returns on capital stay at 8%.

**"Scale and profit" quietly became "maintain our market position."** In FY2024 Lu described a philosophy shift from "scale first" to "long-term sustainable high-quality growth." By FY2025, under cost pressure, the revealed priority is share: "we want to maintain our market position. That is very important to us." The 2022-era philosophy did not survive its first real test.

Note also the interpreter's currency errors throughout the earlier calls ("JPY365.9 billion" for RMB) — a transcription artifact, not a signal, but a reason to trust the reported financials over the transcript text.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not because the strategy is wrong or the team is weak — on the evidence, neither is true — but because every hard number turned at once: revenue −10.9% in Q1 2026 (the first decline in nearly three years), net income −57%, operating profit ~−70%, smartphone shipments −19.2% (worst among the top five), connected-devices revenue −24%, and a car division back in the red at ~USD 5,600 per vehicle after two profitable quarters. Free cash flow was already falling 33% before the shock.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *This is not a company-specific problem, and that is exactly why it is dangerous.* Xiaomi's earnings are down because artificial-intelligence data centres are outbidding phone makers for memory. That means a position in Xiaomi is, mechanically, a **short position on the AI capital-expenditure cycle wearing a consumer-electronics disguise** — the same single shared factor our current regime read names as the dominant risk in the book, with the "memory tax" explicitly identified as the driver of the USD 1.3 trillion semiconductor drawdown of 23–25 June. The thesis does not resolve on anything Xiaomi does. It resolves when memory supply loosens, which analysts now place at **mid-2027** and which has already been pushed back once. A director must decide whether they want that macro exposure at all before deciding whether they like this company — and must not double-count it against other AI-linked positions.

The second consideration: **the market has not capitulated.** The shares are down about 54% from the July 2025 high, yet 23 of 30 analysts still rate the stock a buy against an average target of HKD 39.52. A drawdown without a sell-side surrender is a falling knife, not a washed-out value setup.

### Economic moat

**Moat type: intangible-brand plus scale-cost, with a thin ecosystem switching-cost layer** (1 billion-plus connected devices, HyperOS, 15,000+ owned stores, and now in-house silicon). It is real — 22 consecutive quarters in the global top three is not luck, and the retail network genuinely lowers customer-acquisition cost across phones, appliances and cars.

**Width: NARROW. Trend: ERODING.** The returns evidence does not support anything wider. Return on invested capital of 8.0% and return on equity of 10.9% are, at best, at the cost of capital — Xiaomi has never earned an excess return, in five years of superb growth. And the memory shock ran the definitive experiment: **a company with a wide moat passes a cost shock to its customers. Xiaomi ate it** — margins collapsed, and it lost 19.2% of its shipments anyway, ceding share to Samsung and Apple, who have the balance-sheet depth and the pricing power to absorb the same input inflation. The moat is thin enough that the FY2025 gross margin of 22.3% should be read as a **cyclical peak, not a base** — consistent with our own data showing margins 1.16 standard deviations above their historical peak.

### Secular threat

**Threat: MANAGEABLE. This is a cyclical input shock, not a terminal impairment — and the distinction is the whole investment case.**

The bear temptation is to file Xiaomi under artificial-intelligence displacement. That would be an analytical error. Generative AI is not eating Xiaomi's demand; it is **outbidding Xiaomi for a component**. Nobody is buying fewer phones because of a chatbot. Memory is a notoriously cyclical commodity with a well-documented history of capacity responding to price, and every supplier on earth is now incentivised to build fabs. The demand base is not melting: revenue grew 25% in 2025, the car business is compounding off a genuinely new franchise, and the connected-device installed base is intact.

The honest structural caveats are milder ones: the phone market is mature by management's own admission ("entered a mature phase with overall market showing little growth"), and the car business enters a Chinese price war with real competition. Neither impairs terminal value; both cap it.

**Verdict on the cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a value trap — a cyclical trough that is not yet cheap enough.** At ~18x trailing earnings and ~30x trailing free cash flow, on earnings that have already fallen 57% and on a 2026 consensus that still embeds a 550,000-car year that H1 arithmetic contradicts, the shares are **not** priced for terminal decline. They are priced for a recovery that requires a commodity cycle to turn on schedule. The balance sheet (RMB 66.8 billion of net cash) and the buyback mean this is a survivable wait, not a solvency risk. But being early into a cost squeeze that analysts expect to persist through mid-2027, against a consensus that has not yet marked down its car numbers, is not a margin of safety. It is a timing bet on somebody else's capital-expenditure cycle.
